introduction: “Do not worship the Lantern—worship the light.” These readings argue that scripture speaks in figures and that taking the figures for the thing has kept people from every new teacher: the stars did not fall, the Messiah came from Nazareth, the bread was called flesh. They also say the reverse, that the gates of interpretation should be shut and the clear meaning held, and that everyone’s reading is coloured by himself. Both halves have a long history. Origen asked who could imagine days without a sun; Augustine could not read the Bible until Ambrose showed him that the letter kills; Peter at Pentecost took Joel’s darkened sun as fulfilled; the rabbis said that the Torah speaks in the language of men, and also that no verse leaves its plain meaning; Aquinas founded every sense on the literal. The readings speak hard words about Jewish and Catholic readers, so those readers are given their say here: Maimonides, who called the wolf and the lamb a parable; Paul, who asks whether God has cast away His people; and the Gospel words on which the Eucharist rests.
questions: The readings ask both that the “gates of interpretation” be closed and that scripture never be taken literally. Using the Qur’an’s distinction between clear and allegorical verses and Aquinas’s rule about the literal sense, how would you state a consistent position?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes that every person’s interpretation is coloured by his own individuality, and Blake that two readers find black and white in the same Bible. What, in these readings, is supposed to settle a disputed meaning?

Origen and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá make the same argument about days before the sun. Why has that kind of reading been easier to accept for Genesis than for the resurrection, where Luke has Jesus say “handle me, and see”?

The readings say that the Jews of Jesus’ day knew only the letter. Maimonides read Isaiah’s wolf and lamb as a parable and required no miracles of the Messiah, and Paul warned Gentile Christians not to boast. How should a reader today handle the readings’ language about another people’s way of reading?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls transubstantiation a non-essential; John’s sixth chapter and Paul’s warning are why others hold it essential. What would it take for each side to describe the other’s reading fairly?
“Your lover must love you, not your house.” Which attachments in your own way of reading, to wording, to a tradition, to a favourite interpretation, might be the house?

outside.why: “Do not worship the Lantern—worship the light.” John’s Gospel says it of its first witness: he was not that Light, but was sent to bear witness of that Light.

“The heavenly teachings are expressed in parable in order to be understood and preserved.” Mark: without a parable spake he not unto them; and when they were alone, he expounded all things to his disciples.
This is the verse ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes as plainly symbolic: the mountains and the hills shall break forth into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.
“In the scripture we read that Zion is dancing.” The psalm of the Exodus: the mountains skipped like rams, and the little hills like lambs.

“There are terms and expressions of usage in every language which cannot be taken literally.” The rabbis had a rule for it, which Maimonides later made a principle: the Torah spoke in the language of men.

Passages that conform to reason are taken in “their outward meaning”, and the others have interpretations. Aquinas allowed several senses in scripture and insisted on an order among them: all are founded on the literal, from which alone an argument can be drawn. Who decides, in the reading’s scheme, which passages need interpreting?

“The people of truth … have carefully examined this blessed verse and unraveled therein other far-reaching meanings”, while confirming the literal ones. Ben Bag Bag: turn it over, and turn it over, for all is therein.

“Close fast the gates of interpretation and cleave unto the clear meaning of the Book.” The Talmud records the day a learned rabbi grasped the same rule: a verse does not depart from its literal meaning.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá gives the counsel as binding. The Second Letter of Peter sets a like limit: no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
This is the verse ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes: some verses are clear, the substance of the Book, and others allegorical; those in whose hearts is doubt pursue the allegorical.

“Take not from the Book that which is ambiguous therein, but take what God hath made firm.” Deuteronomy: the secret things belong unto the Lord; those which are revealed belong unto us, that we may do all the words of this law.

“Some of the servants make their own interpretations to justify certain things as lawful.” The Second Letter of Peter says it of Paul’s letters: things hard to be understood, which the unlearned and unstable wrest.
Interpreters bent a verse “to make it conform with those ancient principles accepted by the people”. Jesus: ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition.
“Every person’s interpretation of the Book is colored by his own individuality.” Blake: both read the Bible day and night, but thou read’st black where I read white.

If every reader colours the Book, who is to say what it means? Socrates noticed that a written text, asked a question, gives one unvarying answer and cannot defend itself. What do these readings offer as the answer to his difficulty?
“One who holdeth fast to a single letter, turning away from the Most Great Book.” Jesus: ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel.
This is the saying ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains, with the hearers’ reaction: how can this man give us his flesh to eat?
“By the Bread of Heaven Christ meant the Heavenly Benediction.” At the end of the same discourse Jesus gives a key: the flesh profiteth nothing; the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá argues from the Gospel itself that the food was not material. The Gospels show Jesus making the same correction when the disciples took “leaven” to mean bread.
“The supper of that night became designated as the ‘Lord’s Supper’.” These are the words spoken at it.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá is reported as calling the priests’ claim about the bread a cause of irreligion. Catholic teaching rests it on words like these, which grow more physical when the hearers object: my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed. How would each side say the other reads this chapter?

Transubstantiation is called “a non-essential … imitation and the reverse of reality”. Paul’s warning about eating “not discerning the Lord’s body” is why millions have held it essential. What is at stake for a believer in whether the bread is a sign or more than a sign?
“The assertion that the Son of man came down from heaven has a mystical rather than a literal meaning.” This is the verse: no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven.

The resurrection, says ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, “expresses a spiritual rather than a material condition”. Luke’s account seems written to exclude that: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have. How might the reading’s rule about inner meanings be applied to a passage that insists on the outer?
For Paul everything hung on this: if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain. He also wrote of a “spiritual body”. Does his own language leave room for the reading’s account?
“The story about the dove is simply a metaphor. No dove came down.” Matthew’s wording already has a “like”: the Spirit of God descending like a dove.
This is the passage ‘Abdu’l-Bahá cites for the meaning of Gabriel: the True Spirit brought it down upon thy heart.

“Satan signifieth the powers of nature, which … are expressed as the insistent self.” Paul describes that adversary from the inside, without naming a devil: the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do.
An unbeliever said that Jesus “thought He could see all the world from the top of a mountain”. This is the passage; no mountain shows all kingdoms, which is the reading’s point.
If Adam’s sin were charged to Abraham and Moses, “it would be sheer injustice”. Ezekiel had laid down the principle: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls the inherited guilt of Adam, literally taken, beyond what any rational person can accept. Paul’s sentence is where the doctrine starts: by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin. What is Paul claiming, and what later readers added, is the question the reading raises.
The child who dies unbaptized “has not sinned and goes from this world quite free”. Jesus of children: of such is the kingdom of heaven.

“The statement that God created the heaven and the earth in six days is symbolic.” Origen made the argument in the third century, in nearly the words of the next reading: who that has understanding will suppose that the first days existed without a sun?
The story of Adam and the tree is “all symbols”. Paul reads another story of Genesis that way and says so: which things are an allegory.
“How could we conceive of a day if no sun existed in the heavens?” This is the passage in question: the lights that divide day from night are made on the fourth day.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá suggests that a dynasty’s years were later taken for one man’s. The longest of those lives: all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty and nine years.
This is the account ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says “has an inner meaning”: darkness, the veil rent, the graves opened. He adds: “Our purpose is not to deny.”

Each community denies the others’ miracles, so “either all must be taken literally … or all must be interpreted allegorically”. Hume had used the same symmetry to a different end, as a reason to believe none. What turns the argument toward allegory and away from his conclusion?
“Had such a wonderful thing happened as the parting of the physical sea, it would also have been recorded” in Egypt. This is the record that Israel kept.

“The miracles of Christ were spiritual teachings, not literal.” John’s Gospel, which tells the most physical of the stories, ends by ranking sight below it: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed. Does that verse support the reading or resist it?
Asked for a house of gold or an ascent into heaven, the Prophet of the Qur’an answers: am I aught save a mortal messenger?
“These signs have inner meanings and should not be taken literally.” Jesus’ own example: Elias is come already, and they knew him not.
The verses on the Hour “are all allegorical, and none knows their interpretation save God and those well-grounded in knowledge”. Daniel: the words are closed up and sealed till the time of the end.
This is the passage whose literal reading, Bahá’u’lláh argues, kept people from every Prophet: “they did not see the sun darken, or the stars of heaven fall”.
The New Testament does what the reading asks. Peter at Pentecost quotes Joel on the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood, and says: this is that.

Christian divines “have clung to the literal interpretation of the words of Jesus”. They had texts that invite it: he cometh with clouds, and every eye shall see him. If such a verse is a figure, what is it a figure of?

They would reject anyone who taught “contrary to the letter of the law of the Gospel”. The loyalty the reading blames has scripture behind it: ye shall not add unto the word which I command you. How is a believer to tell faithfulness from being veiled?
What the divines missed, according to the reading, was a promise of one to come. Christians read this verse of the Holy Spirit; Muslims and Bahá’ís have read it otherwise.
They “became deprived of the streaming grace of the Muḥammadan Revelation”. The Qur’an says that Jesus announced it: a messenger who cometh after me, whose name is the Praised One.
People bound to the letter of one law refuse the next. Jesus’ dry remark on it: no man also having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better.
“The Messiah should come from an unknown place, yet we all know this man’s house in Nazareth.” John records the objection: when Christ cometh, no man knoweth whence he is.
“He shall rule with a rod of iron.” The text is the second psalm.
“I possess sovereignty, but it is of the eternal type. It is not an earthly empire.” Jesus to Pilate: my kingdom is not of this world.
“My sword is My tongue.” The Apocalypse draws the same picture, sword and iron rod together: out of his mouth goeth a sharp sword.
“The meaning of an iron scepter … is the tongue.” Isaiah had already put the rod there: he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth.

They expected that the Messiah “would break the mountains apart and cause a mighty earthquake”. The text is Isaiah’s prayer: oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, that the mountains might flow down at thy presence.
“The body of Jesus came from Nazareth”, and so they could not accept him. John: shall Christ come out of Galilee?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that the Jews, taking the signs literally, concluded “this Promised One is not that Promised One”. The greatest codifier of Jewish law taught that the Messiah need work no wonders at all. What, then, were the objections that Jewish teachers thought decisive?

“The Jews held tenaciously to hereditary interpretations.” Maimonides, within that inheritance, read Isaiah’s wolf and lamb as “a metaphor and a parable”. How does his example complicate the picture of a people who knew only the letter?

“All the words of the prophets were fulfilled.” The promise most often cited in reply is this one: nation shall not lift up a sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more. In what sense do the readings hold it fulfilled, and what remains to be done?
“The outward meaning of the verses was the cause of their hinderance.” Paul uses the figure these readings use: a veil on the heart in the reading of the old testament.

The reading speaks with great severity of those who “clung unto the literal text of the Torah”. Paul, a Pharisee by training, guards against the conclusion Christians later drew: hath God cast away his people? God forbid. How should passages like this reading be read after the history that followed such words?
Peter, addressing the people of Jerusalem weeks after the crucifixion, does not say malice: I wot that through ignorance ye did it, as did also your rulers.

“The Jewish doctors have interpreted the Bible according to their own selfish desires.” Paul’s warning to Gentile believers who talked this way: boast not against the branches; thou bearest not the root, but the root thee.
Some read scripture “like parrots, without understanding their inner meanings”. The Dhammapada: one who recites much and does not act on it is like a cowherd counting the cows of others.
“Had reading sufficed, all the Jewish people should have acknowledged Christ.” Paul at Antioch: they knew not the voices of the prophets which are read every sabbath day.

“It is difficult to comprehend even the words of a philosopher; how much more … the Words of God.” Isaiah: the vision is become as the words of a book that is sealed; the learned cannot read it, for it is sealed, nor the unlearned, for he is not learned.

Many “had memorized the texts … and repeated them night and day” without their meanings. The psalmist, who loves the law, knows that reading it is not yet seeing it: open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law.
Those who first received the teachings “understood them literally”. Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel: how can a man be born when he is old? can he enter the second time into his mother’s womb?

The fathers of the Christian religion “gave to the world his literal speech, without explaining the meaning”. Emerson told the divinity students of Harvard the same: churches are not built on his principles, but on his tropes.

“The holy books are full of significance and must never be taken literally.” Deuteronomy says of its commandment that it is not hidden, nor far off, but very nigh, that thou mayest do it. Which parts of a scripture lose their force if they are not taken at their word?
“To penetrate the inner significances a mighty effort is needed.” Proverbs: it is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.
Scripture speaks of “a heaven and an earth other than the physical heaven and earth”. Isaiah: behold, I create new heavens and a new earth.
John saw it too: a new heaven and a new earth, the first passed away, and no more sea.
“Your lover must love you, not your house.” Juliet: ’tis but thy name that is my enemy; a rose by any other name would smell as sweet.
Those who look at “the old dawning places” miss the Sun when it rises elsewhere. John: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
Many “occupied themselves day and night with reciting divine books” and remained veiled. James: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
“They have seized upon the outer meanings of what was revealed in the Book and remained veiled from Him Who revealed it.” Jesus: ye search the scriptures, and ye will not come to me.
This is the verse ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes: the likeness of the ass carrying books.
“All the veiled peoples clung to the literal meanings of their Books.” Jesus: had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me.
“This obstinate people are like the spider: whatever veil of theirs thou dost tear away, they straightway weave another.” The Qur’an’s spider builds a house, the frailest of all houses.
The interpreters “with the axe of conjecture carve out idols of fancy, then bow down before their own handiwork”. The psalm: they that make them are like unto them.
Bacon’s account of the mind’s idols explains how conjecture becomes conviction: what a man had rather were true he more readily believes.
Here it is the interpreters, not the literalists, who are blamed. Antonio: the devil can cite Scripture for his purpose.
“For a thousand years and more, imaginary creatures … were gazing toward … an imaginary city.” Plato’s prisoners watch the wall and give names to the shadows.
“For one thousand two hundred years they disputed about the Qá’im, the Guardian, the Successor.” Paul to Corinth: every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos. Is Christ divided?
A prayer is recited by people who “understand it not”. Jesus: use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do.
“They recite the Qur’an while being heedless of its proof. They pray night and day.” Isaiah: this people draw near me with their mouth, but have removed their heart far from me.
In the ages of obscurity “the nations held blindly to traditions”. Kant’s name for leaving them: man’s release from his self-incurred tutelage.

“The religionists of the world have forsaken the essence of the teaching and hold to the letter.” Augustine could not accept the Bible until he heard Ambrose open it by this rule: the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
“The reality of religion hidden beneath the symbolic forms.” Emerson observed that every word for a spiritual fact was first a word for a material one: spirit primarily means wind.
If religion speaks in symbols, reading it is a skill. Aristotle: the greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor.

“You cannot always take the literal interpretation of first-century Syria or eighth-century Arabia and say in its application it is true now.” Jesus: the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath.

Things are revealed “according to the capacity of the questioner”. Milton’s angel explains his method to Adam: what surmounts the reach of human sense, I shall delineate by likening spiritual to corporal forms.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s example is the Qur’an’s story of Dhu’l-Qarnayn and of Gog and Magog, which he says was “revealed allegorically according to their understanding”, since the questioners conceived it so.

“With these people whose eyes and ears are shut you must be gentle and patient.” The Second Letter to Timothy: be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves.
“Their eyes were holden and they could not see.” The phrase is Luke’s, and he uses it of two disciples who loved Jesus and walked beside him unknowing.

matthew-leaven-of-the-pharisees.text: Then Jesus said unto them, Take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees

john-lazarus-sleepeth.text: Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep. Then said his disciples, Lord, if he sleep, he shall do well. Howbeit Jesus spake of his death: but they thought that he had spoken of taking of rest in sleep. Then said Jesus unto them plainly, Lazarus is dead

mark-without-a-parable.text: And with many such parables spake he the word unto them, as they were able to hear it. But without a parable spake he not unto them: and when they were alone, he expounded all things to his disciples

john-spoken-in-proverbs.text: These things have I spoken unto you in proverbs: but the time cometh, when I shall no more speak unto you in proverbs, but I shall shew you plainly of the Father

corinthians-vail-upon-their-heart.text: But their minds were blinded: for until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament; which vail is done away in Christ. But even unto this day, when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart. Nevertheless when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away

peter-hard-to-be-understood.text: even as our beloved brother Paul also according to the wisdom given unto him hath written unto you; As also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction

peter-private-interpretation.text: Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost

psalm-open-thou-mine-eyes.text: Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law

proverbs-dark-sayings.text: A wise man will hear, and will increase learning; and a man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels: To understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings

proverbs-conceal-a-thing.text: It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter

psalm-mountains-skipped.text: The sea saw it, and fled: Jordan was driven back. The mountains skipped like rams, and the little hills like lambs

ezekiel-doth-he-not-speak-parables.text: Then said I, Ah Lord God! they say of me, Doth he not speak parables

isaiah-book-that-is-sealed.text: And the vision of all is become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed, which men deliver to one that is learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I cannot; for it is sealed: And the book is delivered to him that is not learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I am not learned

corinthians-not-discerning-the-body.text: Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body

john-flesh-is-meat-indeed.text: Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you. Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day. For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed. He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him

luke-flesh-and-bones.text: And as they thus spake, Jesus himself stood in the midst of them, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you. But they were terrified and affrighted, and supposed that they had seen a spirit. And he said unto them, Why are ye troubled? and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have

matthew-like-a-dove.text: And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him

romans-by-one-man.text: Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned

genesis-lights-in-the-firmament.text: And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years: And let them be for lights in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth: and it was so. And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also. And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth, And to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness: and God saw that it was good. And the evening and the morning were the fourth day

peter-one-day-as-a-thousand-years.text: But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day

genesis-methuselah.text: And all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty and nine years: and he died

matthew-veil-was-rent.text: Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice, yielded up the ghost. And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent; And the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose, And came out of the graves after his resurrection, and went into the holy city, and appeared unto many

exodus-sea-divided.text: And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea; and the Lord caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. And the children of Israel went into the midst of the sea upon the dry ground: and the waters were a wall unto them on their right hand, and on their left

john-not-seen-and-yet-believed.text: Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed

psalm-rod-of-iron.text: Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession. Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel

john-no-man-knoweth-whence.text: But, lo, he speaketh boldly, and they say nothing unto him. Do the rulers know indeed that this is the very Christ? Howbeit we know this man whence he is: but when Christ cometh, no man knoweth whence he is

isaiah-rend-the-heavens.text: Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, that thou wouldest come down, that the mountains might flow down at thy presence, As when the melting fire burneth, the fire causeth the waters to boil, to make thy name known to thine adversaries, that the nations may tremble at thy presence

revelation-sword-of-his-mouth.text: And out of his mouth goeth a sharp sword, that with it he should smite the nations: and he shall rule them with a rod of iron

isaiah-rod-of-his-mouth.text: But with righteousness shall he judge the poor, and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth: and he shall smite the earth: with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked

acts-spoken-by-the-prophet-joel.text: But this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel; And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams: And on my servants and on my handmaidens I will pour out in those days of my Spirit; and they shall prophesy: And I will shew wonders in heaven above, and signs in the earth beneath; blood, and fire, and vapour of smoke: The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and notable day of the Lord come

matthew-not-knowing-the-scriptures.text: Jesus answered and said unto them, Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God

acts-read-every-sabbath.text: For they that dwell at Jerusalem, and their rulers, because they knew him not, nor yet the voices of the prophets which are read every sabbath day, they have fulfilled them in condemning him

acts-through-ignorance.text: And now, brethren, I wot that through ignorance ye did it, as did also your rulers

romans-hath-god-cast-away.text: I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew

romans-boast-not-against-the-branches.text: And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert grafted in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree; Boast not against the branches. But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee

john-not-that-light.text: There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. The same came for a witness, to bear witness of the Light, that all men through him might believe. He was not that Light, but was sent to bear witness of that Light

romans-weak-in-the-faith.text: Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations

timothy-in-meekness-instructing.text: And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth

quran-similitude-of-a-gnat.text: Lo! Allah disdaineth not to coin the similitude even of a gnat. Those who believe know that it is the truth from their Lord; but those who disbelieve say: What doth Allah wish (to teach) by such a similitude? He misleadeth many thereby, and He guideth many thereby; and He misleadeth thereby only miscreants;

quran-all-kinds-of-similitudes.text: And verily We have coined for mankind in this Qur'an all kinds of similitudes, that haply they may reflect;

quran-easy-to-remember.text: And in truth We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; but is there any that remembereth?

quran-spiders-house.text: The likeness of those who choose other patrons than Allah is as the likeness of the spider when she taketh unto herself a house, and lo! the frailest of all houses is the spider's house, if they but knew.

quran-mortal-messenger.text: Or thou have a house of gold; or thou ascend up into heaven, and even then we will put no faith in thine ascension till thou bring down for us a book that we can read. Say (O Muhammad): My Lord be Glorified! Am I aught save a mortal messenger?

quran-gog-and-magog.text: They said: O Dhu'l-Qarneyn! Lo! Gog and Magog are spoiling the land. So may we pay thee tribute on condition that thou set a barrier between us and them?

quran-true-spirit-upon-thy-heart.text: And lo! it is a revelation of the Lord of the Worlds, Which the True Spirit hath brought down Upon thy heart, that thou mayst be (one) of the warners, In plain Arabic speech

maimonides-wolf-is-a-metaphor.text: Although Isaiah 11:6 states: 'The wolf will dwell with the lamb, the leopard will lie down with the young goat,' these words are a metaphor and a parable
maimonides-wolf-is-a-metaphor.author: Moses Maimonides

rights.note: Translation published at Sefaria under a CC BY-NC licence.

maimonides-no-miracles-required.text: One should not presume that the Messianic king must work miracles and wonders, bring about new phenomena in the world, resurrect the dead, or perform other similar deeds. This is definitely not true
maimonides-no-miracles-required.author: Moses Maimonides

rights.note: Translation published at Sefaria under a CC BY-NC licence.

augustine-ambrose-letter-kills.text: with delight I heard Ambrose, in his sermons to the people, oftentimes most diligently recommend this text as a rule —The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life; while, drawing aside the mystic veil, he spiritually laid open that which, accepted according to the letter, seemed to teach perverse doctrines
augustine-ambrose-letter-kills.author: Augustine of Hippo

aquinas-founded-on-the-literal.text: all the senses are founded on one — the literal — from which alone can any argument be drawn, and not from those intended in allegory
aquinas-founded-on-the-literal.author: Thomas Aquinas
aquinas-founded-on-the-literal.translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province

origen-without-a-sun.text: For who that has understanding will suppose that the first, and second, and third day, and the evening and the morning, existed without a sun, and moon, and stars? And that the first day was, as it were, also without a sky? … And who is so foolish as to suppose that God, after the manner of a husbandman, planted a paradise in Eden, towards the east
origen-without-a-sun.author: Origen

milton-spiritual-to-corporal.text: and what surmounts the reach / Of human sense, I shall delineate so, / By likening spiritual to corporal forms, / As may express them best
milton-spiritual-to-corporal.author: John Milton

aristotle-command-of-metaphor.text: But the greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor. This alone cannot be imparted by another
aristotle-command-of-metaphor.author: Aristotle

emerson-built-on-his-tropes.text: The idioms of his language, and the figures of his rhetoric, have usurped the place of his truth; and churches are not built on his principles, but on his tropes
emerson-built-on-his-tropes.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

blake-black-where-i-read-white.text: Both read the Bible day and night; / But thou read'st black where I read white
blake-black-where-i-read-white.author: William Blake
